119603.m: The pump moves one positive charge outwards with each cycle.

119604.q: The sodium-potassium pump is a textbook example of which type of transport across the membrane?
119604.e: The pump moves ions against their concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP directly to do so. In diffusion and osmosis, by contrast, particles move without using energy.
119604.m: The sodium-potassium pump is an example of active transport.

119605.q: Which group of drugs blocks the sodium-potassium pump and is used for heart failure?
119605.e: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin from foxglove block the pump in heart muscle cells. This indirectly raises the calcium in the cell, and the heart beats more strongly.
119605.m: Cardiac glycosides slow down the sodium-potassium pump.

119606.q: What happens in the long run if the sodium-potassium pump of a nerve cell is blocked?
a: The resting potential becomes more negative.
119606.e: Without the pump, leak currents gradually even out the concentrations inside and outside. This also removes the basis for resting and action potentials.
119606.m: Without the pump, nerve cells lose their ion gradients.

119607.q: In which structure of the cell is the sodium-potassium pump located?
119607.e: The pump is a transmembrane protein of the plasma membrane. Only there can it transport ions between the inside of the cell and the outside.
119607.m: The sodium-potassium pump sits in the cell membrane.

119609.q: Is the sodium-potassium pump directly needed for a single action potential to run quickly?
a: No, it only maintains the gradients.
Yes, it opens the sodium channels.
Yes, it creates the voltage peak.
No, it only works in muscles.
119609.e: During an action potential only very few ions flow, so the gradients hardly change. The pump restores the concentrations over a longer time.
119609.m: The pump keeps up the supply, not the single impulse.

119610.q: Into which space are neurotransmitters released at a chemical synapse?
119610.e: The vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release the transmitter into the narrow synaptic cleft. From there it diffuses to the receptors of the next cell.

119611.q: Which ion triggers the release of neurotransmitters when an action potential arrives?
119611.e: At the axon terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open. The calcium flowing in makes vesicles fuse with the membrane.
119611.m: Calcium gives the starting signal for transmitter release.

119612.q: Which neurotransmitter is the most important excitatory messenger in the brain?
119612.e: Glutamate is released at most excitatory synapses in the central nervous system. It acts, among others, through AMPA and NMDA receptors.
119612.m: Glutamate is the brain's main driver.

119613.q: Which neurotransmitter is the most important inhibitory messenger in the brain?
119613.e: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) opens chloride channels and makes the next cell harder to excite. Many sedatives strengthen this effect.
119613.m: GABA is the brain's most important brake.

119614.q: How does the nerve poison botulinum toxin (Botox) act at the synapse between nerve and muscle?
a: It prevents the release of the messenger
It increases the release of the messenger
It makes the muscle twitch constantly
119614.e: Botulinum toxin cuts proteins that are needed to release acetylcholine. The muscle no longer receives a signal and stays paralysed.
119614.m: Botox blocks signals from nerve to muscle.

119615.q: Which messenger is released at most sympathetic nerve endings on the target organs?
119615.e: The postganglionic fibres of the sympathetic nervous system mainly release noradrenaline. It raises, for example, heart rate and blood pressure.
119615.m: The sympathetic nervous system mostly acts on organs through noradrenaline.

119616.q: What does an inhibitory neurotransmitter do to the next cell?
a: It makes it harder to excite
It triggers an action potential immediately
It passes the signal on faster
119616.e: Inhibitory messengers such as GABA or glycine usually open chloride channels. The next cell moves further away from the threshold for an action potential.
119616.m: Inhibitory messengers slow down the next cell.

119617.q: What is a small depolarisation of the next cell caused by an excitatory transmitter called?
119617.e: EPSP stands for excitatory postsynaptic potential. Several EPSPs can add up over time and space until the threshold for an action potential is reached.
119617.m: An EPSP brings the next cell closer to the threshold.

119618.q: Which gas acts as an unusual messenger in the nervous system and is not stored in vesicles?
119618.e: Nitric oxide (NO) is made when needed and diffuses freely through membranes. It can even act backwards, from the receiving cell to the sending cell.
119618.m: Nitric oxide is a gaseous messenger.

119619.q: From which amino acid is dopamine made in the body?
119619.e: Tyrosine is first hydroxylated by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, then dopamine is formed in a second step. The body can also make tyrosine from phenylalanine.
119619.m: Dopamine is made from the amino acid tyrosine.

119620.q: In which brain structure do mainly dopamine-producing nerve cells die in Parkinson's disease?
119620.e: The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra in the midbrain control movement through the striatum. When they die, tremor, muscle stiffness and slowness of movement develop.
119620.m: In Parkinson's, dopaminergic cells in the substantia nigra die.

119621.q: Where does dopamine act as a messenger in the nervous system?
a: At the synapses between nerve cells
119621.e: Dopamine is released at synapses and binds to receptors on the next nerve cell. In this way it passes on signals.
119621.m: Dopamine passes on signals at synapses.

119622.q: Why are Parkinson's patients given L-dopa instead of dopamine directly?
a: Dopamine does not pass the blood-brain barrier.
Dopamine is poisonous in the stomach.
119622.e: Dopamine itself hardly gets from the blood into the brain. L-dopa is taken up by a transporter and only converted into dopamine in the brain.
119622.m: L-dopa smuggles dopamine across the blood-brain barrier.

119623.q: Which brain system that uses dopamine is especially linked to reward and motivation?
119623.e: Dopaminergic neurons run from the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens. This reward system also plays an important role in addiction.
119623.m: The mesolimbic system is the brain's reward system.

119624.q: Which messenger is made in the body directly from dopamine?
119624.e: The enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts dopamine into noradrenaline. Adrenaline can in turn be made from noradrenaline.
119624.m: Dopamine is the precursor of noradrenaline.

119625.q: Which group of substances does dopamine belong to?
119625.e: Dopamine contains a catechol ring with two hydroxyl groups and an amino group. Like noradrenaline and adrenaline, it counts as a catecholamine.

119626.q: How do many drugs such as cocaine act on the brain's reward system?
a: They increase the amount of dopamine at the synapses
They immediately destroy all nerve cells
119626.e: Cocaine stops dopamine from being taken back up into the nerve cell. The reward system is strongly stimulated, which can contribute to addiction.
119626.m: Many drugs work through an excess of dopamine.

119627.q: From which amino acid is serotonin made?
119627.e: Tryptophan is converted into 5-hydroxytryptophan and then decarboxylated to serotonin. Tryptophan is an essential amino acid from food.

119628.q: What job does serotonin have in the brain?
a: It acts as a messenger between nerve cells
It forms the sheath of nerve fibres
119628.e: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter. It is released at synapses and influences mood, sleep and appetite, among other things.
119628.m: Serotonin is a messenger in the nervous system.

119629.q: Where is most of the serotonin in the human body?
119629.e: By far the largest part is made by enterochromaffin cells in the gut lining. There it stimulates gut movement.
119629.m: Most serotonin is in the gut.

119630.q: What does the drug group SSRI stand for?
119630.e: SSRIs block the transporter that takes serotonin back from the synaptic cleft. They are mainly used against depression.
119630.m: SSRIs make serotonin work longer in the synaptic cleft.

119631.q: Which mental illness is a lack of serotonin often linked with?
119631.e: Many medicines against depression increase the amount of serotonin in the synaptic cleft. However, the causes of depression are varied and not just a lack of serotonin.
119631.m: Serotonin plays a part in depression.

119632.q: Which hormone is made from serotonin in the pineal gland?
119632.e: In the pineal gland, serotonin is converted into melatonin, mainly at night. Melatonin influences the sleep-wake rhythm.
119632.m: The sleep hormone melatonin is made from serotonin.

119633.q: Why is serotonin often called the “happiness hormone”?
a: It is only made when you laugh
It is only made when you eat chocolate
119633.e: In the brain, serotonin affects mood, calmness and well-being. The term “happiness hormone” is, however, a big simplification.

119634.q: Why does serotonin from food hardly affect your mood?
a: It does not get through the blood-brain barrier
It is completely destroyed in the mouth
It is not found in any food
119634.e: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain and hardly lets serotonin from the blood through. The brain therefore has to make its own serotonin from tryptophan.
119634.m: The brain makes its own serotonin.

119635.q: What is a node of Ranvier?
a: a gap between two sections of myelin
a ring of synapses on the cell body
a bundle of glial cells in the cortex
119635.e: The myelin sheath does not cover the axon without gaps. At the nodes, the axon membrane is exposed.
119635.m: At the node, the axon membrane is exposed without myelin.

119636.q: Who is the node of Ranvier named after?
119636.e: The Frenchman Louis-Antoine Ranvier described the constrictions in the 1870s. He was a doctor and histologist in Paris.
119636.m: Louis-Antoine Ranvier gave the node its name.

119637.q: Which ion channels are found especially densely at the nodes of Ranvier?
119637.e: The high density of sodium channels allows a new action potential to be created at every node. Under the myelin, by contrast, there are hardly any such channels.
119637.m: Nodes are densely packed with sodium channels.

119638.q: How do the nodes of Ranvier affect the conduction of nerve signals?
a: The signal jumps from node to node and so becomes faster
The signal is stopped at every node
The signal becomes slower at the nodes
The signal runs backwards at the nodes
119638.e: New action potentials only form at the nodes; the myelin insulates in between. This jumping, saltatory conduction is much faster than in fibres without myelin.
119638.m: Thanks to the nodes, the signal jumps quickly along the axon.

119639.q: What is the myelinated section of an axon between two nodes of Ranvier called?
119639.e: Between every two nodes there is an internode. It is wrapped by a single myelin-forming cell.
119639.m: An internode lies between two nodes.

119640.q: In the peripheral nervous system, a node lies between two cells of which type?
119640.e: In the peripheral nervous system, each Schwann cell forms a piece of myelin around an axon. Where two Schwann cells meet, a node forms.
119640.m: In peripheral nerves, Schwann cells form the myelin between the nodes.

119641.q: In which group of animals are nodes of Ranvier typically found?
119641.e: Myelinated axons with nodes are a feature of vertebrates. Most invertebrates have no comparable myelin.

119642.q: Which disease destroys myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord and so disturbs conduction between the nodes?
119642.e: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin. The signal can then no longer jump properly from node to node, causing paralysis or vision problems.
119642.m: In multiple sclerosis the myelin is damaged.

119643.q: What does the Latin word “saltare”, from which “saltatory” comes, mean?
119643.e: The signal seems to jump from node to node. Hence the name saltatory conduction.

119644.q: Roughly how fast can fast myelinated nerve fibres in humans conduct?
119644.e: Thick, well myelinated fibres reach around 100 metres per second. That is about 360 km/h.
119644.m: Myelinated fibres conduct at up to about 100 metres per second.

119645.q: What is conduction in axons without a myelin sheath called?
119645.e: Without myelin, a new action potential has to form at every point of the membrane. The signal therefore travels on without gaps and slowly.

119646.q: Roughly how fast do thin unmyelinated C fibres conduct in humans?
119646.e: Thin fibres without myelin only conduct at about 0.5 to 2 m/s. They carry, for example, dull, slow pain.
119646.m: Unmyelinated C fibres are slow lines.

119647.q: What energy advantage does saltatory conduction have?
a: Fewer ions have to be pumped back.
No ATP is needed at all any more.
The nerve cell needs no oxygen.
119647.e: Because ions only flow at the nodes, the overall ion exchange is much smaller. The sodium-potassium pump therefore has less work to do.

119648.q: What physical effect does the myelin sheath have on the axon?
a: It conducts current like a wire.
119648.e: Myelin consists of many layers of lipids and increases membrane resistance. At the same time it lowers capacitance, so the signal is passed on passively far and fast.
119648.m: Myelin works like the insulation on a cable.

119649.q: How do squid without myelin achieve fast conduction for their escape reaction?
a: through a very large axon diameter
119649.e: A thicker axon has a lower internal resistance, so current flows further. The squid's giant axon can be up to about one millimetre thick.
119649.m: Without myelin, only a thick axon helps for fast conduction.

119650.q: A signal travels at 100 m/s along a nerve fibre 1 m long. How long does it take?
119650.e: Time is distance divided by speed: 1 m / 100 m/s = 0.01 s. That is 10 milliseconds.
119650.m: At 100 metres per second, a signal takes ten milliseconds for one metre.

119651.q: Glial cells wrap many nerve fibres in a fatty sheath. What is this sheath called?
119651.e: The myelin sheath insulates the nerve fibre electrically. As a result, the signal jumps from node to node and is passed on much faster.
119651.m: The myelin sheath made by glial cells speeds up nerve conduction.

119652.q: What job do glial cells have in the nervous system in general?
a: They support, supply and protect the nerve cells
They carry all sensory signals to the brain on their own
They form the bones of the skull
They carry oxygen in the blood
119652.e: Glial cells hold the nerve cells in place, supply them with nutrients, insulate nerve fibres and fight off germs.
119652.m: Glial cells are the helper cells of the nerve cells.

119653.q: Glial cells called astrocytes help build a protective barrier of the brain. What is it called?
119653.e: The blood-brain barrier only lets certain substances from the blood into the brain. Astrocytes wrap the brain's blood vessels with their end feet.
119653.m: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain from many substances in the blood.

119654.q: Certain glial cells line the cavities of the brain and spinal cord. Which fluid fills these cavities?
119654.e: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles of the brain and surrounds the brain and spinal cord. It cushions knocks and transports substances.
119654.m: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the cavities of the brain.

119655.q: What does the Greek word “glia”, from which the name glial cell comes, mean?
119655.e: Glial cells used to be thought of as a kind of putty holding the neurons together. Today we know that they have many active jobs.

119656.q: Which scientist coined the term neuroglia as “nerve putty” in the 19th century?
119656.e: In the middle of the 19th century, the Berlin pathologist Rudolf Virchow described a connecting substance between the nerve cells. He called it neuroglia.
119656.m: Rudolf Virchow gave neuroglia its name.

119657.q: What is a brain tumour that starts from glial cells called?
119657.e: Gliomas arise from abnormal glial cells such as astrocytes or oligodendrocytes. Glioblastoma is an especially malignant form.
119657.m: A glioma is a tumour of glial cells.

119658.q: According to newer estimates, what is the ratio of glial cells to nerve cells in the human brain?
a: about ten times more glial cells
about a hundred times more glial cells
about ten times fewer glial cells
119658.e: For a long time it was assumed that there were ten times more glial cells than neurons. Newer counts give a ratio of roughly one to one for the whole brain.
119658.m: The brain has about as many glial cells as nerve cells.

119659.q: According to a well-known learning rule, what happens to the connection between two nerve cells that are often active at the same time?
119659.e: The psychologist Donald Hebb described this rule in 1949. In short: “cells that fire together, wire together”. This is how firm connections form when we learn.
119659.m: Nerve cells active together strengthen their connection.

119660.q: What happens to a synapse that is used often and strongly during learning?
119660.e: Frequently used synapses become more effective over hours to weeks. Experts call this long-term potentiation; it is considered the basis of learning.

119661.q: Which brain region is especially important for forming new memories?
119661.e: The hippocampus lies deep in the temporal lobe. If it is damaged on both sides, people can hardly store new memories any more.
119661.m: The hippocampus helps form new memories.

119662.q: What mainly changes in the brain when we learn something new?
119662.e: When we learn, synapses are strengthened, weakened or newly formed. This ability to change is called neuroplasticity.
119662.m: Learning changes the connections between nerve cells.

119663.q: According to current knowledge, can the adult brain still make new nerve cells?
a: Yes, but only in a few regions such as the hippocampus
Yes, everywhere and in large numbers
Only in the cerebellum during sleep
119663.e: Newly formed neurons have been found in adults in a part of the hippocampus. How much new formation there is in humans is still being researched.
119663.m: Even the adult brain makes new neurons in a few regions.

119664.q: What is a time window in development called in which the brain is especially easy to shape for certain experiences?
119664.e: Hubel and Wiesel showed that an eye covered during an early phase can later hardly use the visual cortex. Similar time windows exist, for example, for learning languages.
119664.m: In critical periods the brain is especially easy to shape.

119665.q: Can synapses also become weaker on purpose during learning?
119665.e: Besides strengthening, there is also a lasting weakening of synapses, called long-term depression. Together they allow networks to be fine-tuned.
119665.m: Synapses can also be weakened on purpose.

119666.q: Which phenomenon after an amputation is linked with a reorganisation of the cerebral cortex?
119666.e: After an amputation, neighbouring areas of the body map in the cortex take over the area that has become free. This reorganisation can cause sensations in the missing limb.
119666.m: Phantom pain shows how the cerebral cortex reorganises itself.

119667.q: Who first recorded an electroencephalogram of a human in Jena in 1924?
119667.e: The psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded brain waves in 1924 and published them in 1929. He also introduced the name electroencephalogram.
119667.m: Hans Berger is considered the inventor of the EEG.

119668.q: Which waves does the EEG typically show when you are relaxed and awake with your eyes closed?
119668.e: Alpha waves of about 8 to 13 Hz occur when you are calmly awake with your eyes closed. When you open your eyes, they usually become weaker.
119668.m: Relaxed with eyes closed, the EEG shows alpha waves.

119669.q: Which EEG waves below 4 Hz are typical of deep sleep?
119669.e: Delta waves are slow waves with a high amplitude. They mark the deepest stages of sleep.
119669.m: In deep sleep, slow delta waves dominate.

119670.q: Which EEG waves of about 13 to 30 Hz occur during focused mental activity?
119670.e: Beta waves have a higher frequency and a smaller amplitude. They show an active, attentive brain.
119670.m: Focused thinking produces fast beta waves.

119671.q: According to which international system are EEG electrodes arranged on the scalp?
119671.e: In the 10-20 system, the electrodes are placed at distances of 10 or 20 per cent of certain distances across the head. This makes measurements comparable for different head sizes.
119671.m: The 10-20 system sets the electrode positions.

119672.q: In which order of magnitude is the voltage of EEG signals measured on the scalp?
119672.e: The signals are only a few to about a hundred microvolts strong. That is why sensitive amplifiers are needed.
119672.m: EEG signals are tiny voltages in the microvolt range.

119673.q: For diagnosing which disease is the EEG especially important?
119673.e: In epilepsy, the EEG often shows typical spikes and sharp waves. This makes it possible to identify where seizures start and what kind they are.
119673.m: The EEG is a key tool in epilepsy.

119674.q: What does an EEG with electrodes on the scalp record?
a: The electrical activity of many nerve cells of the cerebral cortex
The blood flow in the brain's vessels
The oxygen content in the brain
The tension of the neck muscles
119674.e: Nerve cells of the cerebral cortex produce tiny electric currents when they work. When very many are active at the same time, their sum can be measured on the scalp as a brain wave curve.
119674.m: The EEG measures the brain waves of many nerve cells at once.

119675.q: What kind of disease is multiple sclerosis?
119675.e: In MS, the body's own immune system attacks the myelin sheaths. This creates areas of inflammation and scars.
119675.m: In MS, the immune system turns against the body's own nervous system.

119676.q: Which part of the nervous system is affected in multiple sclerosis?
a: only the nerves of the skin
119676.e: MS affects the central nervous system, meaning the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. Peripheral nerves are usually spared.
119676.m: MS is a disease of the central nervous system.

119677.q: Roughly what is the ratio of women to men in multiple sclerosis?
a: Women are affected about 2 to 3 times more often.
Men are affected about 3 times more often.
Both are affected exactly equally often.
119677.e: Like many autoimmune diseases, MS affects women much more often. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood.
119677.m: MS affects far more women than men.

119678.q: Which course of multiple sclerosis is most common at the start?
119678.e: In most patients, relapses occur first, which clear up completely or partly. Later this can turn into a progressive course.

119679.q: Which imaging method shows MS lesions in the brain best?
119679.e: On MRI, the areas of inflammation in the white matter are clearly visible. It is therefore central to diagnosis and to checking how the disease develops.

119680.q: At what age does multiple sclerosis usually begin?
119680.e: The disease usually appears in young adulthood. It is a common cause of neurological disability in young adults.
119680.m: MS often begins in young adulthood.

119681.q: Why can MS symptoms temporarily get worse in the heat, for example in a hot bath?
a: Damaged nerve fibres conduct even worse when warm
Heat thins the blood in the brain
119681.e: In fibres with a damaged myelin sheath, conduction becomes less reliable at higher temperatures. When the body cools down, the symptoms improve again.
119681.m: In MS, heat can make symptoms worse for a short time.

119682.q: Which inflammation is a common first sign of multiple sclerosis?
119682.e: Optic neuritis causes blurred vision and pain when moving the eyes. In many patients it is the first symptom.
119682.m: Optic nerve inflammation can be the first sign of MS.

119782.q: In ecology, what is meant by a bioindicator?
a: A living thing whose presence or condition shows environmental conditions
A chemical device for measuring pollutants in the air
A substance that artificially speeds up plant growth
A bacterium that completely breaks down pollutants
119782.e: Bioindicators react sensitively to certain environmental factors. Their presence, absence or condition therefore tells you something about the quality of air, water or soil.
119782.m: A bioindicator is a living thing that shows environmental conditions.

119783.q: What is the system called that assesses water quality using organisms with different tolerances of organic pollution?
119783.e: The saprobic system ranks water organisms by their tolerance of organic pollution that uses up oxygen. The species found give a saprobic index.
119783.m: The saprobic system assesses waters by the organisms living there.

119784.q: What distinguishes an accumulation indicator from a reaction indicator?
a: It builds up pollutants in its tissue, which can be measured
It dies immediately at the slightest pollution
It only shows changes in temperature
It only grows in completely unpolluted areas
119784.e: Accumulation indicators such as some mosses store pollutants, for example heavy metals, without visibly suffering. Reaction indicators, by contrast, show damage or disappear.
119784.m: An accumulation indicator stores pollutants that can be detected in the laboratory.

119785.q: What does the presence of many stonefly larvae in a stream show?
119785.e: Stonefly larvae need cool water rich in oxygen. That is why they are among the indicators of good water quality.
119785.m: Stonefly larvae only live in clean streams rich in oxygen.

119786.q: Which animals, in large numbers on the bottom of a body of water, show heavy organic pollution with little oxygen?
119786.e: Sludge worms (Tubifex) can stand very little oxygen and live in rotting mud. If they appear in huge numbers, a body of water is heavily polluted.
119786.m: Many sludge worms point to a heavily polluted body of water.

119787.q: What is the structure of a diatom's shell made of two halves often compared to?
a: A honeycomb pattern made of wax
119787.e: The shell consists of a larger upper half (epitheca) and a slightly smaller lower half (hypotheca). These fit into each other like a box with a lid.
119787.m: A diatom's shell consists of two halves like a box and lid.

119788.q: What effect does cell division in many diatoms have on the size of the offspring?
a: Some of the cells get smaller with each division
All cells get bigger with each division
The cells fuse together again afterwards
The shell dissolves completely at each division
119788.e: Each daughter cell builds a new, smaller lower half inside the old half of the shell. As a result, the average cell size decreases over many divisions.
119788.m: In diatoms, divisions make the cells smaller on average over time.

119789.q: How do diatoms regain their full size after shrinking through many divisions?
a: A special cell grows without a rigid shell
Two shells fuse into a larger one
They add lime from the water
The shell expands in warm conditions
119789.e: Once a minimum size is reached, an auxospore forms. It grows without a rigid shell and then forms a large cell again.
119789.m: A special cell without a rigid shell restores the full size of diatoms.

119790.q: Which material is formed from the deposited shells of fossil diatoms?
119790.e: Diatomaceous earth (diatomite) is a fine, porous rock made of diatom shells. Alfred Nobel used it to soak up nitroglycerine in dynamite.
119790.m: Diatomaceous earth consists of the shells of dead diatoms.

119791.q: Which two basic shapes of diatoms can be distinguished under the microscope?
119791.e: Centric diatoms are radially symmetrical and often round like a tin. Pennate forms are elongated and bilaterally symmetrical, rather like a little boat.
119791.m: Diatoms are either round or elongated.

119792.q: Why are diatoms golden brown rather than green, even though they contain chlorophyll?
a: A brown extra pigment masks the green
They have no chlorophyll at all
Their lime shell is coloured brown
They take up soil from the water
119792.e: The pigment fucoxanthin, a carotenoid, masks the green of the chlorophyll. It also helps to capture blue-green light. The shell is made of silicon dioxide, not lime.
119792.m: A brown extra pigment makes diatoms golden brown.

119793.q: How do many elongated diatoms move slowly over stones and mud?
a: They glide on mucus they secrete
They push off with gas bubbles
119793.e: They secrete mucus through a long slit in the shell called the raphe. This lets them glide slowly over surfaces.

119794.q: Why are cyanobacteria, once called “blue-green algae”, not true algae?
a: They are prokaryotes without a cell nucleus
119794.e: Cyanobacteria are bacteria and have no true cell nucleus. True algae, by contrast, are eukaryotes.
119794.m: Cyanobacteria are bacteria, not true algae.

119795.q: What ability of cyanobacteria led to the Great Oxidation Event around 2.4 billion years ago?
119795.e: During photosynthesis, cyanobacteria split water and release oxygen. As a result, oxygen built up in the atmosphere.
119795.m: Through photosynthesis, cyanobacteria brought oxygen into the Earth’s atmosphere.

119796.q: What are the layered limestone structures built by mats of cyanobacteria called?
119796.e: Stromatolites form when bacterial mats bind sediment and lime layer by layer. Fossil stromatolites are among the oldest traces of life on Earth.
119796.m: Stromatolites are limestone layers built by cyanobacteria.

119797.q: Which toxin produced by some cyanobacteria mainly damages the liver?
119797.e: Microcystins are toxins that can get into the water during blooms of cyanobacteria. They damage the liver of mammals, which is why swimming warnings may be needed during algal blooms.
119797.m: Microcystin is a liver toxin from cyanobacteria.

119798.q: Why can the water in Swiss lakes such as Lake Zurich sometimes turn reddish?
a: Because of the burgundy blood alga, a cyanobacterium
Because of iron rust from the lake bed
Because of waste water from dye works
119798.e: The burgundy blood alga (Planktothrix rubescens) contains a lot of red pigment. When it multiplies massively, the water can turn reddish.
119798.m: The burgundy blood alga is a reddish cyanobacterium found in lakes.

119799.q: Where does the German name for stoneworts, “Armleuchteralgen” (candelabra algae), come from?
a: From the side branches arranged in whorls, which look like a candelabra
119799.e: The side branches grow in regular whorls at the nodes of the main stem. This makes the plant look like a candelabra with many arms.
119799.m: Stoneworts have whorled branches like a candelabra.

119800.q: Why do many species of the genus Chara feel rough and brittle?
a: They deposit lime on their surface
They are covered in silica needles
They are made of dead wood
119800.e: During photosynthesis, the algae remove carbon dioxide from the water. This causes lime to precipitate and settle on their surface.
119800.m: Many Chara species are covered with a lime crust.

119801.q: What are the very large internodal cells of stoneworts often used for in research?
a: To study cytoplasmic streaming and electrical signals
119801.e: The internodal cells can be several centimetres long. Cytoplasmic streaming is easy to observe in them, and action potentials can be measured.
119801.m: The giant cells of stoneworts are well suited to cell research.

119802.q: Which group do stoneworts belong to?
a: Green algae, closely related to land plants
119802.e: Stoneworts such as Chara and Nitella are green algae. They are among the closest living relatives of land plants.
119802.m: Stoneworts are green algae and close relatives of land plants.

119803.q: What anchors stoneworts in the bed of a lake or river?
119803.e: Stoneworts have no true roots. Colourless rhizoids hold them in the sediment.

119804.q: What does the return of stoneworts to a previously over-fertilised lake indicate?
119804.e: When less phosphate enters a lake, the water becomes clearer. Then stoneworts, which need a lot of light, can form underwater meadows again.
119804.m: Returning stoneworts are a sign of better water quality.

119805.q: How is the shoot of a stonewort divided up?
a: Into nodes and long sections in between, the internodes
Into trunk, crown and veined leaves
119805.e: The main stem consists of short nodes from which the side branches grow. In between are long internodes, which often consist of just one giant cell.
119805.m: Stoneworts consist of nodes and internodes.

119806.q: Which genus forms the peat mosses that build up raised bogs?
119806.e: All peat mosses belong to the genus Sphagnum. They are the most important peat formers in raised bogs.
119806.m: Peat mosses belong to the genus Sphagnum.

119807.q: What is the job of the hyaline cells in the tiny leaves of peat mosses?
a: They carry out most of the photosynthesis
They carry sugar to the roots
119807.e: Hyaline cells are large, empty cells that fill with water. They make peat mosses very effective water stores.
119807.m: In peat mosses, hyaline cells store the water.

119808.q: What does the word “hyaline” originally mean?
119808.e: The word comes from the Greek hyalos, meaning glass. The cells are colourless and translucent.

119809.q: What state are the hyaline cells of a fully grown peat moss leaf in?
a: They are dead and have no living cell contents
They are the only living cells
119809.e: The hyaline cells lose their protoplast as they mature. What remains is the cell wall as a hollow space that can take up water.
119809.m: Fully grown hyaline cells are dead, empty storage cells.

119810.q: Which cells form a narrow network between the hyaline cells in peat moss leaves?
119810.e: Narrow green cells run between the large, empty storage cells. They contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis.
119810.m: The green cells form a network between the hyaline cells.

119811.q: How can water get into the hyaline cells quickly?
a: Through pores in their cell wall
119811.e: The hyaline cells have round openings in their walls. Water flows straight in through these pores.
119811.m: Pores let water flow into the hyaline cells.

119812.q: What stops the empty hyaline cells from collapsing when they dry out?
a: Ring-shaped or spiral thickenings in the wall
High internal pressure caused by salt
119812.e: Reinforcing fibres are built into the walls of the hyaline cells. They support the cells like the rings in a hose.
119812.m: Reinforcing fibres keep the hyaline cells open.

119813.q: Why do dry cushions of peat moss often look whitish?
a: The hyaline cells are then filled with air
The mosses are then covered in snow
The mosses then grow white flowers
119813.e: Hyaline cells filled with water are transparent, so the green of the other cells shows through. Filled with air, they scatter the light and look pale.
119813.m: Air-filled hyaline cells make dry peat mosses look pale.

119814.q: Which other moss also has water-storing hyaline cells and therefore looks bluish white?
119814.e: Leucobryum glaucum has leaves with several layers containing large, empty cells. These give the cushions their pale grey to whitish colour.
119814.m: Leucobryum also stores water in hyaline cells.

119815.q: What does poikilohydry mean in plants and lichens?
a: Their water content adjusts to the humidity of their surroundings
Their water content always stays the same
The plant only takes up salt water
The plant stores water in tubers
119815.e: Poikilohydric organisms can hardly regulate their water balance. They dry out along with their surroundings and quickly take up water again when it is damp.
119815.m: Poikilohydric organisms are as wet or dry as their surroundings.

119816.q: What is the ability of most vascular plants to keep their water content largely constant called?
119816.e: Homoiohydric plants have a cuticle, adjustable stomata and large vacuoles. This lets them keep their water content fairly stable despite changing surroundings.
119816.m: Homoiohydric plants regulate their own water content.

119817.q: What is the “rose of Jericho”, often sold as a ball in shops, known for?
a: It turns green again after drying out completely
It only grows in the dark
It catches insects with sticky traps
119817.e: The false rose of Jericho (a spikemoss) curls up into a ball when it dries out. When given water, it unfolds again within hours and turns green.
119817.m: The rose of Jericho survives drying out completely.

119818.q: What is the state of greatly reduced metabolism called that dried-out mosses or tardigrades enter?
119818.e: In anhydrobiosis, metabolism almost completely stops after water loss. When water returns, the organisms resume their life processes.
119818.m: In anhydrobiosis, organisms survive without water.

119819.q: Which habitat can poikilohydric lichens and mosses colonise thanks to their tolerance of drying out?
a: Bare rocks that are completely dry at times
Only the inside of deep caves
119819.e: On rocks, rain and complete dryness alternate often. Poikilohydric organisms survive this, whereas most vascular plants would dry up there.
119819.m: Mosses and lichens that tolerate drying out also colonise dry rocks.

119820.q: Why do many poikilohydric lichens grow very slowly?
a: They only carry out photosynthesis when damp
They only take in food at night
119820.e: When dry, their metabolism rests. The time in which they can photosynthesise and grow is therefore often short.
119820.m: Lichens grow slowly because they are only active when damp.

119821.q: Which substances help organisms that tolerate drying out to protect their cell parts during water loss?
a: Sugars such as sucrose or trehalose
119821.e: Such sugars replace water at membranes and proteins. When drying out, they form a glassy mass that stabilises the structures.
119821.m: Sugars protect cells when they dry out.

119822.q: Which structures do most mosses lack that would let them actively control water loss like vascular plants?
a: A thick cuticle and adjustable stomata on the leaves
119822.e: Moss leaves are usually only one cell layer thick and barely protected against evaporation. Without adjustable stomata, they lose water quickly to the air.
119822.m: Moss leaves can hardly regulate evaporation.

119823.q: Which three main growth forms of lichens are distinguished?
119823.e: Crustose lichens lie tightly against the surface, foliose lichens form leafy lobes. Fruticose lichens grow upright or hanging and are branched.
119823.m: Lichens grow as crustose, foliose or fruticose lichens.

119824.q: Where do some crustose lichens grow on limestone rocks?
a: In the top few millimetres inside the rock
Only on the underside of leaves
Only in the water of mountain lakes
119824.e: These endolithic lichens live inside the rock itself. From the outside, you often see only discolouration or small fruiting bodies.

119825.q: Roughly how fast does the map lichen grow?
a: Often less than one millimetre per year
119825.e: Crustose lichens are among the slowest-growing living things. Large patches of map lichen can therefore be several hundred years old.
119825.m: The map lichen grows extremely slowly.

119826.q: What do researchers use the very slow-growing map lichen for?
a: To estimate the age of moraines and rockfalls
119826.e: The bigger a lichen patch, the longer the rock has been exposed. This method is called lichenometry and is used, for example, in areas in front of glaciers.
119826.m: Lichens can be used to estimate how long rocks have been exposed.

119828.q: What extra advantage does a cyanobacterium bring as the photobiont of a lichen?
a: It can fix nitrogen from the air
It makes the lichen poisonous to all animals
It makes the lichen move faster
119828.e: Cyanobacteria such as Nostoc not only make sugar but also fix nitrogen from the air. This gives the lichen extra nitrogen.
119828.m: Cyanobacteria also supply the lichen with nitrogen.

119829.q: What does the photobiont supply to the fungal partner of the lichen?
119829.e: Green algae mainly release sugar alcohols such as ribitol, cyanobacteria rather glucose. The fungus feeds on this and in return provides protection and water.
119829.m: The photobiont supplies the fungus with sugar.

119830.q: What did the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener discover about lichens in the 19th century?
a: They consist of a fungus and an alga
They are a special kind of moss
119830.e: Schwendener interpreted the green cells in the lichen as algae living together with a fungus. His theory was fiercely disputed at first but is now considered confirmed.
119830.m: Lichens are a partnership between a fungus and an alga.

119831.q: Where is the photobiont located in a layered lichen?
a: In an algal layer under the upper cortex
In the anchoring threads at the bottom
119831.e: In layered lichens, a fungal cortex protects the algal layer beneath it. This way the photobiont gets light but is protected from drying out and strong radiation.
119831.m: The photobiont usually lies in a layer under the cortex.

119832.q: What advantage do cyanobacteria bring as partners in some lichens?
a: They fix nitrogen from the air
They protect the lichen from being eaten
They spread the lichen by spores
119832.e: Cyanobacteria can fix nitrogen from the air and make it available to the lichen. This is a big advantage in nutrient-poor places such as rocks or tree bark.
119832.m: Cyanobacteria supply some lichens with nitrogen from the air.

119833.q: What do the powdery soredia contain, which many lichens use to spread vegetatively?
a: Fungal threads and cells of the photobiont
119833.e: Soredia are tiny granules of algal cells wrapped in fungal threads. This way, both partners reach a new place together.
119833.m: Soredia spread the fungus and photobiont together.

119834.q: Where does the common liverwort grow particularly often?
a: In damp, nutrient-rich places such as the edges of fountains
In the crowns of tall spruces
119834.e: The common liverwort needs a lot of moisture and likes nutrient-rich places. It can be found at fountains, on stream banks, on garden paths and in garden centres.
119834.m: The common liverwort loves damp, nutrient-rich places.

119835.q: What does the body of the common liverwort look like?
a: A flat thallus that branches into forks
An upright stem with spirally arranged leaves
A long thread made of one row of cells
119835.e: The common liverwort is a thalloid liverwort. Its flat thallus branches into forks again and again.
119835.m: The common liverwort forms a flat, forked thallus.

119836.q: What are the small openings on the upper side of the thallus?
a: Air pores leading to air chambers
Guard cells that open and close
119836.e: The air pores lead into air chambers with cells rich in chloroplasts. Unlike stomata, they cannot close.
119836.m: The common liverwort has air pores that cannot close.

119837.q: Why is the common liverwort an important model organism in plant research?
a: It is easy to grow and its genome has been sequenced
It is the largest plant in the world
It lives for several thousand years
It does not carry out photosynthesis
119837.e: Marchantia grows quickly and is easy to keep in the laboratory. Since its genome was published in 2017, it has been well suited to studying the evolution of land plants.
119837.m: Marchantia serves as a model plant for the evolution of land plants.

a: Long-term monitoring of the environment using living things
A one-off count of all animals in a zoo
119838.e: In biomonitoring, organisms are studied repeatedly to detect changes in the environment. This makes it possible to follow trends over years.
119838.m: Biomonitoring watches the environment over a long time using living things.

a: Test organisms are deliberately placed at measuring sites
Only organisms that grow there naturally are studied
Only instruments without living things are used
119839.e: In active biomonitoring, standardised organisms such as moss bags or grass cultures are placed at measuring sites. In passive biomonitoring, the species that occur there naturally are studied.
119839.m: In active biomonitoring, test organisms are deliberately put out.

119840.q: Which pollutants are mainly measured in Europe-wide moss monitoring?
a: Heavy metals such as lead and cadmium
119840.e: Mosses take up substances directly from rain and dust and accumulate them. Analysing them shows how much heavy metal is deposited from the air.
119840.m: Mosses show the deposition of heavy metals from the air.

119841.q: What is the name of the federal programme that has systematically monitored Switzerland’s biodiversity since 2001?
119841.e: In Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland (BDM), plants, butterflies, birds and other groups are recorded regularly on fixed sample areas. This makes it possible to detect changes in biodiversity.
119841.m: Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland keeps track of biodiversity.

119842.q: Which organisms does the Swiss IBCH index use to assess rivers and streams?
a: Small invertebrates on the stream bed
119842.e: The IBCH is based on macroinvertebrates, meaning insect larvae, snails, worms and crustaceans. Their composition shows the biological quality of a stream.
119842.m: The IBCH assesses streams by their small invertebrates.

119843.q: In biomonitoring, how can you tell that ozone-sensitive tobacco plants are exposed to high ozone levels?
a: By pale spots on the leaves
119843.e: Sensitive tobacco varieties such as Bel W3 develop typical pale spots when ozone levels are high. The extent of the spots shows the level of pollution.
119843.m: Ozone causes pale spots on sensitive tobacco leaves.

119844.q: What is the advantage of biomonitoring compared with a single chemical measurement?
a: It shows the overall effect of pollution over a longer period
It is always more accurate for single substances
119844.e: Living things react to the interplay of many factors over weeks or years. A chemical sample, by contrast, only shows one moment.
119844.m: Biomonitoring shows the effect of pollution on living things over time.

119845.q: What is studied with the environmental DNA (eDNA) method?
a: Traces of genetic material from living things in water or soil samples
The colour of leaves under UV light
The body size of captured animals
119845.e: Animals and plants leave skin cells, mucus or droppings in their surroundings. The DNA in them can be used to work out which species are present without catching them.
119845.m: With environmental DNA, species are detected from traces of genetic material.

119846.q: Which three large groups of mosses does bryology distinguish?
119846.e: True mosses usually have a leafy stem. Liverworts are leafy or thalloid, and hornworts have horn-shaped spore capsules.
119846.m: Bryophytes are divided into mosses, liverworts and hornworts.

119847.q: Roughly how many species of moss have been described worldwide?
119847.e: After flowering plants, mosses are one of the most species-rich groups of land plants. About 16,000 species are known worldwide.
119847.m: There are about 16,000 moss species worldwide.

119848.q: What is the name of the national data and information centre for the mosses of Switzerland?
119848.e: Swissbryophytes collects records and knowledge about the mosses of Switzerland. It is based at the University of Zurich.
119848.m: Swissbryophytes is the data centre for Swiss mosses.

119849.e: Bryology is the study of mosses. The name comes from the Greek “bryon”, meaning moss.
119849.m: Bryology is the science of mosses.

119850.q: What are organisms called that only tolerate a narrow range of an environmental factor and are therefore particularly good bioindicators?
119850.e: Stenoecious species have a narrow ecological tolerance. If a factor changes only a little, they disappear, which shows the change clearly.
119850.m: Stenoecious species are good bioindicators because of their narrow tolerance.

119851.q: Why are amphibians considered sensitive bioindicators?
a: They have permeable skin and live both in water and on land
They have a very thick armour
119851.e: Amphibians easily absorb water and dissolved substances through their thin skin. They also depend on intact waters and land habitats.
119851.m: Thanks to their permeable skin, amphibians react sensitively to environmental toxins.

119852.q: Why are mussels often used to monitor pollutants in water?
a: They filter a lot of water and accumulate pollutants in their tissue
They change colour immediately when there are pollutants
They leave polluted water by flying away
They break down all pollutants completely
119852.e: Mussels filter large amounts of water for food. Heavy metals and other substances build up in their bodies and can be measured.
119852.m: Mussels store pollutants from the water they filter.

119853.q: What substance is the shell of a diatom made of?
119853.e: The shell, called a frustule, is made of silicon dioxide, the same substance as quartz and glass. That is where the German name “Kieselalge” (silica alga) comes from.
119853.m: Diatoms build their shells from silicon dioxide.

119854.q: In what form do diatoms store some of their energy?
119854.e: Diatoms do not make starch. They store energy as oil droplets and as a soluble carbohydrate. Deposited marine algae contributed to the formation of crude oil over millions of years.

119855.q: Biologically speaking, what is the “spirulina” sold as a food supplement?
a: A dried seaweed with a cell nucleus
119855.e: Spirulina consists of the spiral threads of the cyanobacterium Arthrospira. They are grown in tanks and dried.
119855.m: Spirulina is a cyanobacterium, not a true alga.

119856.q: How do some thread-like cyanobacteria survive unfavourable times such as winter in lake sediment?
119856.e: Some cyanobacteria form enlarged cells with thick walls and many reserves, called akinetes. They survive in the sediment and germinate again later.
119856.m: Resting cells help cyanobacteria survive bad times.

119857.q: What do many planktonic cyanobacteria use to regulate how deep they float in the water?
a: Oil drops on the outside of the thread
119857.e: Gas vesicles are gas-filled protein shells that provide buoyancy. By building them up and breaking them down, the cells control the depth at which they float.
119857.m: Gas vesicles let cyanobacteria float in the water.

119858.q: How do dense stands of stoneworts benefit a lake?
a: They bind nutrients, stabilise the sediment and keep the water clear
They raise the water temperature a lot
They drive away all the fish
They turn the water red for swimmers
119858.e: The underwater meadows take up nutrients and stop mud from being stirred up. They also provide a habitat for small animals and young fish.
119858.m: Stoneworts help to keep lakes clear.

119859.q: What is the dense tuft of young branches at the tip of a peat moss stem called?
119859.e: At the tip, the young branches are packed closely together and form a head. This is where the peat moss keeps growing while it dies off below.
119859.m: Peat mosses keep growing at their head.

119860.q: How are the branches arranged along the stem of a peat moss?
a: In clusters of spreading and hanging branches
Singly and opposite each other, as in the stinging nettle
Only at the base as a ring of roots
Not at all, peat mosses are unbranched
119860.e: Peat mosses bear clusters of branches in which some branches spread out and others hang close to the stem. The hanging branches carry water upwards.
119860.m: Peat mosses bear their branches in clusters.

119861.q: How does the round spore capsule of a peat moss spread its spores?
a: It shoots off the lid and spores explosively using air pressure
It is carried away by ants
It opens slowly with a ring of teeth
It falls into the water and floats away
119861.e: As it dries, the capsule shrinks and the pressure of the trapped air rises. Finally the lid pops off and the spores are shot upwards as if from an air gun.
119861.m: Peat moss capsules shoot out their spores with air pressure.

119862.q: In mosses such as peat moss, what is the green, long-lived moss plant called?
119862.e: In mosses, the green plant is the gametophyte. The spore capsule is the sporophyte, which sits on it and is fed by it.
119862.m: In mosses, the green plant is the gametophyte.

119863.q: Why are plant remains hardly broken down in raised bogs?
a: It is wet, acidic and low in oxygen
119863.e: Peat mosses make their surroundings acidic and hold a lot of water. In the wet, acidic, oxygen-poor environment, decomposers barely work, and so peat forms.
119863.m: An acidic, wet bog slows decomposition and lets peat form.

119864.q: What is the aim of growing peat mosses on rewetted bog land?
a: To obtain peat moss as a renewable substitute for peat in potting compost
To use peat mosses as cattle feed
To produce fuel for power stations
119864.e: In this paludiculture, freshly grown peat mosses are harvested instead of digging up old layers of peat. This keeps the carbon stored in the peat in the ground.
119864.m: Cultivated peat mosses can replace peat in potting compost.

119865.q: What do fully grown peat mosses lack, unlike most other mosses?
119865.e: Only very young peat mosses have rhizoids. Later they grow without anchorage in dense cushions and take up water over their whole surface.
119865.m: Fully grown peat mosses have no rhizoids.

119866.q: How quickly do many dried-out mosses resume photosynthesis after being moistened?
a: Often within minutes to a few hours
119866.e: Mosses that tolerate drying out keep their cell structures intact when dry. After being wetted, they can therefore quickly carry out photosynthesis again.
119866.m: Many mosses become active again soon after rain.

119867.q: Why can a crustose lichen hardly be removed from a stone without destroying it?
a: Its underside is firmly grown into the surface
It is stuck on with tree resin
It has deep roots in the rock
It is frozen on by the rain
119867.e: Crustose lichens have no lower cortex. Their fungal threads grow directly into the top layer of the surface. Foliose lichens, by contrast, can often be lifted off.
119867.m: Crustose lichens are firmly grown into their surface.

119868.q: Why were almost all lichens missing in the past from cities with heavy sulphur dioxide pollution?
a: Lichens absorb pollutants unfiltered from air and rain
Lichens need a lot of sulphur dioxide to grow
There are no stones in cities
119868.e: Lichens have no roots and no protective waxy layer. They take up water and dissolved substances over their whole surface. Only a few species such as Lecanora conizaeoides tolerated high pollution.
119868.m: Lichens show how clean the air is.

119869.q: What do the black lines between neighbouring patches of map lichen mean?
119869.e: Each lichen grows with a dark edge of fungal threads without algae, called the prothallus. Where two lichens meet, these edges remain visible as black boundaries.
119869.m: The black lines of the map lichen are boundaries between separate lichens.

119870.q: What do the fruiting bodies of the fungal partner look like in many crustose lichens?
a: Like small discs or little bowls on the thallus
119870.e: These fruiting bodies are called apothecia. In them, the fungus produces spores that are spread without an algal partner.
119870.m: Many crustose lichens bear disc-shaped apothecia.

119871.q: What is the photobiont in a lichen?
a: The partner that carries out photosynthesis
The fungus that forms the thallus
A parasite that harms the lichen
The anchoring thread on the surface
119871.e: The photobiont is a green alga or a cyanobacterium. Through photosynthesis it makes sugar, which the fungal partner also lives on.
119871.m: The photobiont supplies the lichen with sugar through photosynthesis.

119872.q: In what striking way does the common liverwort reproduce asexually?
a: With gemmae in small gemma cups
119872.e: Small cups containing lens-shaped gemmae sit on the thallus. Raindrops splash them out, and new plants grow from them.
119872.m: The common liverwort reproduces with gemma cups.

a: Their lobed thallus reminded people of a liver and was thought to cure it
They contain as much iron as liver
They only grow on dead animals
They used to be made into liver sausage
119873.e: The flat, lobed thallus of some liverworts resembles the shape of a liver. According to old beliefs, they were therefore supposed to help against liver complaints.
119873.m: Liverworts are named after their liver-like shape.

119874.q: What does the common liverwort use to hold on to the ground, although it has no true roots?
119874.e: Mosses and liverworts have no true roots. Fine, root-like threads of cells called rhizoids anchor them in the soil and help to hold water.
119874.m: Mosses and liverworts anchor themselves with rhizoids.

119875.q: Which generation forms the green, long-lived plant in the common liverwort, as in all bryophytes?
119875.e: In bryophytes, the green plant is the gametophyte. The sporophyte stays small and sits on it. In ferns and seed plants, it is the other way round.
119875.m: In bryophytes, the green plant is the gametophyte.

119876.q: Why are honeybees used in biomonitoring?
a: They forage over a large area and bring pollutants into honey, pollen and wax
They measure the air temperature with their antennae
119876.e: A bee colony flies over an area several kilometres across. Residues in honey, pollen or wax therefore give clues about pollution in a whole region.
119876.m: Bees collect samples from a large area.

119877.q: Why do mosses usually stay very short?
a: They have no woody vascular tissue to transport water
They are constantly eaten by animals
119877.e: Mosses lack true vascular tissue with woody cells. Water only travels short distances in the plant, so they stay small.
119877.m: Without vascular tissue, mosses stay short.

119878.q: Which moss genus builds up raised bogs and forms peat?
119878.e: Peat mosses keep growing at the top while they die off below. In the wet, acidic bog, the remains hardly decompose and become peat.
119878.m: Peat mosses build up raised bogs.

119879.q: Why are dried moss specimens in a herbarium easy to identify?
a: They swell up again in water and show their features
They keep their colour unchanged for ever when dry
They are identified only by their smell
119879.e: Mosses are poikilohydric and take up water again even after years. When softened, their leaves and cells show their shape under the microscope almost as if fresh.
119879.m: Dried mosses swell up again in water.

119880.q: Which moss makes its protonema shimmer golden green in cave entrances and rock crevices?
119880.e: The protonema of goblin gold (Schistostega pennata) has lens-shaped cells. They focus the weak light onto the chloroplasts and partly reflect it back.
119880.m: Goblin gold shimmers thanks to lens-shaped cells.

119881.q: Which soil animals are often studied as bioindicators of soil quality and pollution?
119881.e: Earthworms live in close contact with the soil and take it in with their food. Their number, species diversity and pollutant levels show the condition of the soil.
119881.m: Earthworms indicate the condition of a soil.

119980.q: In which lobe of the brain is the prefrontal cortex?
119980.e: The prefrontal cortex forms the very front part of the frontal lobe, directly behind the forehead.
119980.m: The prefrontal cortex is at the very front of the frontal lobe.

119981.q: Which abilities are mainly linked to the prefrontal cortex?
119981.e: The prefrontal cortex controls the so-called executive functions. These include planning actions, making decisions and holding back sudden impulses.
119981.m: The prefrontal cortex is the brain's planning and control centre.

119982.q: Which railway worker survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe in 1848 and afterwards changed a lot in personality?
119982.e: During a blast, an iron rod pierced Phineas Gage's skull. He survived, but was afterwards described as uncontrolled and erratic, which pointed to the role of the frontal lobe in social behaviour.
119982.m: The case of Phineas Gage showed that the frontal lobe helps shape personality.

119983.q: According to current knowledge, up to roughly what age does the prefrontal cortex mature?
119983.e: The prefrontal cortex is one of the brain regions that mature last. The rebuilding processes last into young adulthood, until about the mid-20s.
119983.m: The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain areas to finish developing.

119984.q: Which memory system, which holds and works on information for a short time, depends strongly on the prefrontal cortex?
119984.e: In working memory, information is kept active for seconds, for example during mental arithmetic. Imaging studies show strong activity in the prefrontal cortex at such times.
119984.m: During mental arithmetic, working memory is busy in the frontal lobe.

119985.q: Why is leucotomy, in which nerve pathways to the frontal lobe were cut, now seen as a dark chapter of medicine?
a: It often changed personality and drive severely and permanently
It was too expensive for hospitals
119985.e: The operation made many patients calmer, but often also listless and without drive. Despite a Nobel Prize for Egas Moniz in 1949, it is no longer used today.
119985.m: Leucotomy is now seen as a warning example in medical history.

119986.q: Which messenger is especially important for the prefrontal cortex and is boosted by ADHD medicines such as methylphenidate?
119986.e: Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline. This raises their concentration in the gap between the nerve cells, which can improve attention and impulse control.
119986.m: Methylphenidate increases the amount of dopamine between nerve cells.

119987.q: What is the part of the prefrontal cortex directly above the eye sockets that evaluates rewards called?
119987.e: Orbit is the technical term for the eye socket. The orbitofrontal cortex lies above it and is involved in decisions and in evaluating rewards.
119987.m: The orbitofrontal cortex lies above the eye sockets.

119988.q: Where does the hippocampus get its name from?
a: From the name of its discoverer
From the Latin word for memory
119988.e: Hippocampus is the Greek-Latin name for the seahorse. The curved part of the brain looks like this animal.
119988.m: The hippocampus looks like a seahorse.

119989.q: In which lobe of the brain is the hippocampus?
119989.e: The hippocampus lies on both sides in the inner part of the temporal lobe.
119989.m: The hippocampus sits deep in the temporal lobe.

119990.q: What did the famous patient “H. M.”, who had parts of both hippocampi removed in 1953, show?
a: The hippocampus is needed to form new memories
Without a hippocampus you can no longer see
119990.e: After the operation, H. M. could no longer remember new experiences permanently. Old memories and skills, however, were largely kept.
119990.m: The patient H. M. showed that the hippocampus stores new memories.

119991.q: Which technical term for part of the hippocampus recalls the ram's horns of an Egyptian god?
119991.e: The main part of the hippocampus is called cornu Ammonis, meaning Ammon's horn. Its curled shape recalls the ram's horn of the god Amun.
119991.m: Because of its shape, the hippocampus is also called Ammon's horn.

119992.q: Which cells in the hippocampus, whose discovery earned John O'Keefe the Nobel Prize in 2014, are active in particular places?
119992.e: Place cells fire when an animal is at a particular spot in space. They form a kind of inner map.
119992.m: Place cells in the hippocampus form an inner map.

119993.q: During which phase are memories transferred from the hippocampus to the cerebral cortex especially intensely?
119993.e: In deep sleep, content stored in the hippocampus during the day is replayed. This gradually consolidates it in the cerebral cortex.
119993.m: In deep sleep the brain consolidates what it has learnt.

119994.q: What is meant by adult neurogenesis, which is studied in the hippocampus?
a: The formation of new nerve cells in adulthood
The death of nerve cells in old age
The development of the brain in the embryo
The healing of bones after a fracture
119994.e: For a long time it was believed that no new nerve cells form in the adult brain. New formation has been found in the hippocampus, but how much happens in humans is disputed.
119994.m: New nerve cells can form in the hippocampus even in adulthood.

119995.q: Which sign is typical when the hippocampus is damaged early in Alzheimer's?
119995.e: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus is one of the first brain regions affected. That is why gaps in short-term memory are noticed first.
119995.m: Alzheimer's damages the hippocampus early and with it remembering new things.

119996.q: What does the Greek name amygdala mean?
119996.e: Amygdala is the Greek word for almond. The structure is an almond-shaped group of nuclei in the temporal lobe.
119996.m: Because of its shape, the amygdala is named after the almond.

119997.q: Which feeling is the amygdala most closely linked with?
119997.e: The amygdala checks stimuli for danger in a flash and triggers fear and startle reactions. However, it is also involved in other feelings.
119997.m: The amygdala raises the alarm when there is danger.

119998.q: What did the patient “S. M.”, whose two amygdalae had been destroyed by a rare disease, show?
119998.e: S. M. had the rare Urbach-Wiethe syndrome. Even in dangerous situations she showed hardly any fear, which proves the role of the amygdala in fear.
119998.m: Without the amygdala, the feeling of fear is largely missing.

119999.q: Which functional system of the brain is the amygdala counted as part of?
119999.e: The limbic system processes feelings and is involved in memory. The amygdala and hippocampus, among others, are counted as part of it.
119999.m: The amygdala belongs to the limbic system of feelings.

120000.q: Which brain structure works closely with the amygdala in fear to store memories of dangerous experiences?
120000.e: The amygdala gives memories their emotional colour, the hippocampus stores the context. That is why frightening experiences are often remembered especially well.
120000.m: The amygdala and hippocampus store fear memories together.

120001.q: Why do you often get a fright even before you have consciously recognised a danger?
a: A fast nerve pathway reports stimuli directly to the amygdala
The cerebellum recognises dangers faster than the eyes
The muscles react entirely without the brain
The heart first sends a warning signal to the brain
120001.e: Some sensory stimuli reach the amygdala on a short, rough route, others more slowly through the cerebral cortex. That is why you flinch before you know exactly what is going on.
120001.m: The amygdala reacts to danger before we consciously recognise it.

120002.q: Which form of learning, in which a neutral stimulus is linked with an unpleasant event, depends especially on the amygdala?
120002.e: In fear conditioning, for example, a tone alone causes fear after being paired several times with a frightening stimulus. Without a working amygdala, this link can hardly be made.
120002.m: The amygdala learns which stimuli signal danger.

120003.q: Which stress hormone does the adrenal cortex release when the amygdala starts a hormone chain through the hypothalamus and pituitary during stress?
120003.e: The amygdala activates the hypothalamus, which stimulates the adrenal cortex through the pituitary. This then releases the stress hormone cortisol.
120003.m: Under stress, the amygdala starts a hormone chain that reaches the adrenal cortex.

120004.q: What is the main job of the thalamus?
a: To filter sensory information and pass it on to the cerebral cortex
To learn the fine-tuning of movements
120004.e: The thalamus is a relay station: almost all sensory signals pass through it to the cerebral cortex. That is why it is also called the “gateway to consciousness”.
120004.m: The thalamus is the gateway to consciousness.

120005.q: Which part of the brain does the thalamus belong to?
120005.e: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon. It lies deep inside between the cerebrum and the brainstem.
120005.m: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon.

120006.q: Which is the only sense that is not mainly passed to the cerebral cortex through the thalamus?
120006.e: Smell information goes from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex without first being relayed in the thalamus. All other senses pass through the thalamus.
120006.m: Only smells take the direct route past the thalamus relay station.

120007.q: Through which brain structure do signals from the retina reach the visual cortex in the occipital lobe?
120007.e: The fibres of the optic nerve are relayed in a nucleus of the thalamus, the lateral geniculate body. From there the visual pathways run to the visual cortex.
120007.m: Visual information is also relayed in the thalamus.

120008.q: In a rare prion disease, mainly the thalamus is destroyed. Which ability do people affected increasingly lose?
120008.e: In fatal familial insomnia, misfolded prions mainly destroy nuclei of the thalamus. The people affected increasingly lose the ability to sleep.
120008.m: Without an intact thalamus, sleep can break down.

120009.q: What does the Greek word “thalamos” mean?
120009.e: In Ancient Greek, thalamos meant an inner room or a bedroom. The name suits its hidden position deep in the brain.
120009.m: The thalamus is named after an inner chamber.

120010.q: What can occur on the opposite side of the body after a stroke in the thalamus?
a: Severe pain that is hard to treat
A loss of the sense of smell
120010.e: In thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome), people suffer severe pain on the opposite side of the body after a thalamic stroke, because the thalamus processes sensory signals wrongly.
120010.m: Damage to the thalamus can cause agonising pain.

120011.q: Which method can reduce severe shaking of the hands by having an electrode in the thalamus influence nerve cells electrically?
120011.e: In deep brain stimulation, a thin electrode is placed in a nucleus of the thalamus. Weak electrical pulses can clearly reduce severe shaking, for example in essential tremor.
120011.m: Electrodes in the thalamus can reduce severe shaking.

120012.q: What are the basal ganglia mainly responsible for?
120012.e: The basal ganglia are groups of nuclei deep in the cerebrum. In loops with the cerebral cortex, they promote intended movements and hold back unwanted ones.
120012.m: The basal ganglia choose which movement is carried out.

120013.q: Where in the brain are the basal ganglia?
a: On the surface of the cerebellum
120013.e: The basal ganglia are clusters of nerve cells deep in the cerebrum, below the cortex. They are closely linked through loops with the cerebral cortex and the thalamus.
120013.m: The basal ganglia lie deep in the cerebrum.

120014.q: For which disease of the basal ganglia is deep brain stimulation with implanted electrodes often used?
120014.e: In deep brain stimulation, an electrode is placed permanently in a nucleus of the basal ganglia. In many people with Parkinson's, this eases stiffness and tremor.
120014.m: Deep brain stimulation helps many people with Parkinson's.

120015.q: In which inherited disease with involuntary, sweeping movements do mainly nerve cells in the striatum die?
120015.e: Huntington's disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant way. The loss of nerve cells in the striatum leads to excessive, dance-like movements.
120015.m: Huntington's disease damages the striatum and causes involuntary movements.

120016.q: Which system in the brain, which also includes parts of the basal ganglia, plays a central role in addiction?
120016.e: Part of the basal ganglia belongs to the reward system. Addictive substances activate this system especially strongly, which is why people want them again and again.
120016.m: Addiction is closely linked to the reward system in the brain.

120017.q: Which part of the basal ganglia is called “pale globe” in translation?
120017.e: Globus means globe, pallidus means pale. The globus pallidus looks lighter than its surroundings because of many myelinated fibres.
120017.m: The globus pallidus is the pale globe of the basal ganglia.

120018.q: Which form of learning is especially linked with the basal ganglia?
120018.e: When actions are repeated often, the basal ganglia increasingly take over their control. That is how routines such as brushing your teeth become automatic habits.
120018.m: Habits are anchored in the basal ganglia.

120019.q: Which disorder with motor and vocal tics is linked with a malfunction of the basal ganglia?
120019.e: In Tourette syndrome, involuntary movements and sounds occur. It is thought that disturbed inhibition in the loops of the basal ganglia contributes to this.
120019.m: In Tourette syndrome, the movement selection of the basal ganglia is disturbed.

120020.q: Which messenger is missing in Parkinson's because the cells that make it for the basal ganglia die?
120020.e: In Parkinson's, nerve cells in the substantia nigra that supply dopamine to the basal ganglia die. Without dopamine, movements become slow and stiff.
120020.m: In Parkinson's, the basal ganglia lack dopamine.

120021.q: What job does the corpus callosum have in the brain?
a: It connects the two halves of the brain
It protects the brain from knocks
120021.e: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibres. Through it, the left and right halves of the brain exchange information.
120021.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

120022.q: Which syndrome, in which one hand seems to act on its own, can occur after damage to the corpus callosum?
120022.e: In alien hand syndrome, one hand carries out movements that the person does not intend. It can occur after the corpus callosum is cut or after other brain damage.
120022.m: After damage to the corpus callosum, a hand can seem controlled by someone else.

120023.q: Roughly how many nerve fibres make up the corpus callosum?
120023.e: The corpus callosum contains about 200 to 250 million nerve fibres. This makes it by far the largest fibre connection between the hemispheres.
120023.m: Hundreds of millions of fibres connect the two halves of the brain.

120024.q: For which condition is the corpus callosum sometimes cut by surgery?
120024.e: In a callosotomy, the corpus callosum is cut so that epileptic seizures can no longer spread from one half of the brain to the other. The operation is only considered in severe cases that cannot be treated otherwise.
120024.m: Cutting the corpus callosum can stop seizures from spreading.

120025.q: In which half of the brain are the most important language centres in most people?
120025.e: In most people, especially right-handers, language is processed mainly in the left half of the brain. Experiments with split-brain patients also showed this.
120025.m: Language is usually in the left half of the brain.

120026.q: A split-brain patient sees an object only in the left visual field. What typically happens?
a: He cannot name it, but can find it by touch with his left hand
He can name it, but cannot find it by touch
He does not see the object at all
120026.e: The left visual field is processed in the right hemisphere, while language is usually on the left. Without the corpus callosum, the information does not reach the language centre, but the right half of the brain can control the left hand.
120026.m: Without the corpus callosum, the speaking half of the brain does not know what the other half sees.

120027.q: What was special about the brain of Kim Peek, the real person behind the film “Rain Man”?
a: He had only one brain hemisphere
120027.e: Kim Peek was born with agenesis of the corpus callosum, meaning without a corpus callosum. He had an extraordinary memory for thousands of books.
120027.m: Kim Peek lived without a corpus callosum and had an enormous memory.

120028.q: What is the corpus callosum mainly made of?
120028.e: The corpus callosum is made of nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty myelin layer. This makes the tissue look white.
120028.m: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of white matter.

120029.q: Who is Broca's area named after?
120029.e: In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca described a patient who had lost the ability to speak and had damage in the left frontal lobe. The region has carried his name ever since.
120029.m: In 1861 Paul Broca found a speech centre in the frontal lobe.

120030.q: In which brain hemisphere is Broca's area located in most right-handed people?
120030.e: In over 90 per cent of right-handed people, language is mainly based in the left hemisphere. Broca's area lies there in the lower frontal lobe.
120030.m: In most people, language sits on the left.

120031.q: What could Broca's famous patient still do fairly well despite losing his speech?
120031.e: The patient could hardly speak any more but understood much of what was said to him. From this Broca concluded that speaking is controlled by its own area of the brain.
120031.m: When Broca's area is damaged, understanding is often preserved.

120032.q: How does a person with Broca's aphasia typically speak?
120032.e: In Broca's aphasia, producing speech is a struggle and there is little grammar. Understanding language, on the other hand, is usually fairly well preserved.
120032.m: In Broca's aphasia, speaking is laborious and choppy.

120033.q: Which language centre is mainly responsible for understanding language?
120033.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls speaking. Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is especially important for understanding language.

120034.q: Because of its main disorder, what is Broca's aphasia also called?
120034.e: Broca's aphasia mainly affects the production of speech. That is why it is also called motor or expressive aphasia.
120034.m: Broca's aphasia mainly disturbs speaking itself.

120035.q: What is the most common cause of a sudden loss of language (aphasia) in adults?
120035.e: In a stroke, part of the brain no longer receives blood. If it hits the language centres in the left hemisphere, aphasia can suddenly occur.
120035.m: A stroke can suddenly take away a person's language.

120036.q: What is the leaving out of function words and endings, typical of Broca's aphasia, called?
120036.e: In agrammatism, sentences consist mainly of content words, such as “Me hospital go”. Small words and grammatical endings are missing.
120036.m: Agrammatism is language without the building blocks of grammar.

120037.q: Which doctor described the language centre in the temporal lobe named after him in 1874?
120037.e: In 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke described patients who spoke fluently but hardly understood language. He linked this to a region in the temporal lobe.
120037.m: Carl Wernicke discovered the centre for understanding language.

a: In the rear part of the upper temporal gyrus
In the occipital lobe near the visual cortex
120038.e: Wernicke's area usually lies in the left hemisphere in the rear section of the superior temporal gyrus, close to the auditory cortex.
120038.m: Wernicke's area lies near the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

a: A language disorder after brain damage
